text: I open the spreadsheet on the left monitor and scroll to row forty. I copy the figures from the grey column and paste them into the blank cells below. The cursor blinks after the last number, and I save the file under the same name.

Across the room a printer starts up and begins feeding paper through its tray. I walk over, lift the stack of printed sheets, and count them against the list on my desk. I write the total in the corner of the cover page and clip the copies together with two black binder clips.

Angled toward the keyboard, the desk lamp lights a screen full of unsorted names. I select the column header, open the menu, and choose alphabetical order from the list. Each row shifts up into its new place, and I scroll down to check the last entry.

Before the meeting I sort the printed agenda into two piles, one for the budget and one for the schedule. I staple the budget pages in the top left corner and slide them into a blue folder. The schedule goes into a plastic sleeve, and I set both folders at the empty chair on the far side of the table.

On the second floor I badge through the glass door and walk past the copier to my desk. I unplug the monitor, wind the charging cable around two fingers, and drop it in the top drawer. Then I stack the notebooks by size and turn off the desk lamp.

Next I sign into the expense system and open the form for last week's receipts. I scan each receipt, type its amount beside it, and attach the image to the matching line. The running total updates at the bottom of the screen, and I click submit.

Standing up to fetch a file, I roll the chair back on its five plastic wheels. I open the cabinet by the window, pull out the folder labelled March, and check the tabs against the index card. I close the drawer and return to the screen, where the document is still open.

Two onions sit on the cutting board beside a knife and a bowl of water. I peel the papery skin off each one and cut off the root end. Then I slice both halves into thin strips and scrape them into a steel pan on the stove.

Pasta boils in a tall pot, and the lid lifts a little each time steam escapes. I measure a cup of dried penne, tip it into the water, and set the kitchen timer for nine minutes. When it rings, I drain the pot through a colander in the sink and watch the steam rise past the window.

Between the two burners I set a small saucepan with a thin layer of oil. I crack an egg into a small bowl and slide it into the pan. The white turns opaque at the edges, and I move the spatula underneath to lift it.

Each tortilla goes onto the dry skillet for about thirty seconds per side. I flip them with tongs, stack them on a paper towel, and cover the pile with a folded dish cloth. Two bags of shredded cheese sit open on the counter beside the salsa jar.

From the freezer I take a bag of frozen peas and shake them loose onto a baking sheet. I scatter them in one layer, slide the tray into the oven, and set the dial to two hundred degrees. The oven fan hums, and the light inside stays on for the next twenty minutes.

Once the water reaches a rolling boil I add a handful of salt and drop in the green beans. They sink, rise to the surface, and turn a brighter shade within a minute. I lift them out with a slotted spoon and lay them on a folded towel to drain.

Under the lid the rice has absorbed the water and the pot is no longer bubbling. I fluff the grains with a fork from the edges toward the center, and the steam lifts off in thin white threads. I scoop a portion into a plain bowl and set it on the table next to the teapot.

At the first traffic light I move into the left lane and check the mirror. The engine idles at a steady pitch while the light stays red for a while. When the arrow turns green I press the pedal and merge onto the exit ramp.

Car keys hang from a hook by the back door, and I take them down with my left hand. I adjust the driver seat two notches forward and tighten the belt across my chest. The radio stays off, and the wipers scrape once across the dry windshield before I reverse out of the driveway.

Along the highway the lane markers pass in steady dashes under the headlights. I check the speedometer, which reads sixty-two, and set the cruise control with a button on the wheel. A delivery truck changes lanes ahead, and I keep the same distance behind it.

Behind me the bus pulls away from the curb and the doors fold shut with a hiss. I tap my card on the reader by the bus driver's seat, and the small screen shows the fare. I walk down the aisle and sit by the window, where the glass shows the reflection of the shop signs.

Then the train doors open at the platform, and I step onto the carriage with a bag over my shoulder. I check the route map above the seats, count three stops, and hold the vertical pole near the door. The announcement repeats the next station name in two languages.

Rain taps on the windshield in short bursts while the wipers sweep at the slowest setting. I read the road signs from the dashboard light and turn the car onto the access road by the fuel station. The gravel shoulder runs alongside, and a line of parked trucks sits near the gate.

My bicycle leans against the railing at the station, its front wheel turned toward the bus lane. I unlock the chain, slide it through the spokes, and check the tyre pressure with my thumb. I pedal out onto the cycle path and follow the painted white line past the bakery.

Beside the creek a row of alder trees drops its leaves onto the packed mud. I kneel on a flat stone, dip a metal cup into the shallow water, and watch small bubbles rise from the bottom. The current moves around a fallen branch and splits into two thin streams.

Gravel crunches under my boots as I follow the trail up the ridge. Pine needles cover the path in brown drifts, and a jay calls twice from the branches overhead. At the top I stop beside the cairn, read the metal plaque, and note the elevation on the back of my map.

Rows of corn stand tall on the far side of the fence, and their dry leaves rattle in the breeze. I walk the field edge with a clipboard, count the stalks in each marked square, and write the numbers in pencil. A tractor idles near the barn, and its exhaust drifts across the gravel road.

Overhead a line of geese crosses the grey sky in a loose V, calling at intervals. I stand at the edge of the lake and write the time, the wind direction, and the water level in a notebook. The reeds at my feet are bent flat, and a patch of wet sand shows where the water has pulled back.

Sand shifts under the rope of the tent as the wind pushes steadily from the west. I pull the stake deeper with the mallet, check the guy line for slack, and fold the groundsheet into a square. Inside, the sleeping bags lie flat on the tent floor, and I pull the zipper closed along its track.

Snow falls in small flakes that settle on the bark of the birch trees. I brush the powder off a wooden bench, sit down, and open a thermos of plain water. The path ahead is marked with orange stakes, and footprints from earlier in the morning lead toward the ridge.

Mud covers the lower steps of the wooden boardwalk, so I walk along the middle planks. A heron stands motionless in the marsh about ten metres away, its neck folded against its chest. I raise the camera, focus on the bird, and take one photo before it lifts off.

Dust gathers in a thin grey film along the top of the bookshelf. I wipe each shelf with a dry cloth, moving from left to right, and set the figurines on a towel beside me. The vacuum sits by the hall door with its cord coiled around the handle.

Laundry turns over in the drum with a steady thump and a low hum. I pull a damp shirt from the top of the pile, shake it out once, and hang it on a wooden hanger by the window. Each sock goes into a pair, and I fold the towels into thirds before stacking them on the shelf.

Mop water in the orange bucket is grey and cloudy with dust. I dip the head, wring it twice against the rim, and draw long strokes across the kitchen tiles. Behind me the floor dries in patches, and I move the chairs back to their places one at a time.

Ironing starts with the collar of the blue shirt, pressed flat from the points toward the button. I move on to the cuffs, then the front panels, using long passes of the iron. Finished shirts hang in a row on the back of the bedroom door.

Trash bags line the hallway by the back door, tied shut at the necks. I carry the recycling bin outside, lift the lid, and sort the cardboard flat into the blue container. The kitchen bin gets a fresh liner, and the old one goes out to the curb.

Beds are made in two movements, the sheet pulled tight at the corners and the duvet shaken loose. I tuck the fitted sheet under the mattress on the left side, then cross to the right. Two pillows go into clean cases, and I set them at the head of the bed in a straight line.

Dishes stack in the sink, and the water runs from the tap in a steady stream. I rinse each plate, set it in the wooden rack, and stand the glasses upside down. The sponge goes back on its ledge, and I wipe the counter in short circles until the surface is dry.

The receptionist slides a clipboard across the counter and points to the blank lines. I write my name, date of birth, and the address printed on my card. The pen is clipped to the form, and I return it to the counter.

A nurse wraps the cuff around my upper arm and presses the start button on the monitor. The numbers rise on the small screen, then drop to a steady figure, and she writes them on a chart. She removes the cuff, folds it, and says the doctor will come in next.

Paper crinkles on the examination table whenever I shift my weight. I unbutton the shirt and fold it over the chair back, and the room holds a faint smell of antiseptic from a wall dispenser. The doctor knocks twice and enters with a folder.

Inside the pharmacy, the clerk types my date of birth and checks it against the paper slip. A small white bag holds two amber bottles, each with a printed label and a childproof cap. I sign the screen with a plastic stylus and slide the receipt into my coat pocket.

Facing the far wall, I cover my left eye with a paper card. The eye chart hangs there, and I read its rows of letters aloud from the largest line down to the smallest. The technician marks a grid on her sheet and asks me to switch eyes.

Down the corridor a scale sits in the corner, its flat grey platform worn at the edges. I step onto it in my socks, and the digits settle after a moment. The assistant writes the number beside my name, then measures my height with a sliding bar and asks me to face the wall.

Gauze lies folded in a sterile tray, and the nurse lifts a strip with tweezers. She wipes a small scratch on my hand with a cotton swab and covers it with a square of clear plastic. I flex my fingers once to check the bandage, then look at the wall clock.

Holding the serving spoon, my sister asks where the gravy boat goes. I point to the empty space by the bread basket, and she sets it down beside the potatoes. My father is still carving the roast, and the knife makes a long, even sound on the board.

Four of us sit around the low table in the living room with mugs of tea. Ana reads the scores from her phone while Tomas shuffles the cards. Nobody speaks for a moment as the cards are dealt, and the lamp throws a yellow circle on the rug.

Her daughter sits beside me on the sofa, sorting the photographs into two piles by year. I turn over a print of a beach, check the date pencilled on the back, and place it in the left pile. She slides a box of loose slides across the cushion.

Propped on the hall table, the card has a row of stamps and my cousin's name written in blue ink. I open the envelope with a butter knife, unfold the single sheet, and read the first line again. Then I place it face up beside the clock, next to the box of keys.

Walking the river path, my brother and I take turns holding the dog's lead. Our dog stops every few metres to sniff the grass near the fence. Each time, my brother says her name twice and stands still until she trots ahead. We pass a woman with a stroller and a man folding a newspaper on a low wall.

Last Sunday my aunt carries a tray of cut melon to the garden table and sets it between two bowls of rice salad. The children are drawing chalk squares on the patio, and their voices drift over the hedge. I wipe the table with a damp cloth, fold the napkins into halves, and count the chairs.

Nora writes the address on the envelope in capital letters and sticks a stamp in the corner. I fold the letter in thirds, slide it in, and seal the flap with a damp sponge. We both sign the bottom of the card, and she adds the date in the top right corner.

Half the seats in the lecture hall are taken, and the projector hums above the stage. I copy the table from the slide into my notebook, one row at a time, using a blue pen. When the professor clicks forward, I underline the column headings and write the page number in the margin.

Chalk dust settles on the wooden ledge below the blackboard, and the teacher wipes a corner with the side of her hand. She writes three equations in a column and taps each one with the pointer. The class copies them down, and the clock above the door shows ten past nine.

Index cards cover the library table in three stacks, each held together with a rubber band. I read the first card aloud under my breath, flip it over, and write the answer on the back in pencil. The wall clock ticks above the shelves of bound journals.

Turned face down, the printed worksheet lies on my desk beside a pencil with a sharpened point. I flip the sheet over, write my name in the top corner, and read the first question again. The second question asks for the boiling point of water at sea level, so I draw a small diagram in the margin.

Beneath the bulb on my desk, I run a yellow highlighter along the second paragraph of the chapter. The ink soaks into the thin paper and the words underneath stay readable. When the paragraph is done, I write two short notes in the empty space at the bottom of the page.

In the chemistry lab the burner hisses blue as I adjust the gas valve. I measure 25 millilitres of distilled water into a glass beaker and record the reading in the log. The thermometer clipped to the stand reads 21 degrees, and I write that down too.

Open at chapter four, the history reader rests on the desk beside a bowl of pencils. I copy the dates from the timeline into a grid in my exercise book, with one column for each century. The grid fills the page, and I number each box in the order it appears in the text.

Stretching on the mat, I bend forward from the hips and count thirty seconds on my watch. My palms rest flat on the rubber surface. I switch legs, then roll the foam cylinder under each calf in slow passes toward the knee.

Black ropes with white floats mark the pool lane, and the water is still. I push off the wall, count strokes with each breath, and touch the far end at the tile line. I turn with a tuck, glide, and start the next length.

Jump ropes click against the floor in a steady rhythm as the coach counts the rounds. I land on the balls of my feet, keep my elbows close to my ribs, and turn the handles in small circles. Each round is ten skips, and the coach writes the total on the whiteboard by the door.

Dumbbells rest on the rack in pairs, and the lightest set is closest to the mirror. I pick up the pair of grey weights, sit on the bench, and curl them slowly toward my shoulders for ten repetitions. The mirror shows my elbows moving up and down in the same line. I rack the weights, wipe the bench with a towel, and log the count in a small notebook.

Pedals turn steadily under my feet while the display shows cadence, distance, and minutes elapsed. I keep my back straight, adjust the seat one notch lower, and stare at the wall of framed race photos. A fan spins at the front of the bike, and the air moves across my face.

Medicine balls rest on the floor between two mats, with a stopwatch lying beside them. I stand with my feet apart, lower into a squat, and push up through my heels. Then I pass the ball to my partner, who catches it and passes it back.

Orange cones mark the edges of the training field, spaced about five metres apart. I jog to the first cone, touch its top, and turn back toward the start line. The coach records each lap on a pad, and the wind moves the grass in long slow waves.

Sandpaper rubs the edge of the wooden shelf in short strokes that follow the grain. I brush the loose dust off with the flat of my hand and check the surface against the light. Then I wrap the block in paper and set it on the workbench next to the wood glue.

Solder flows along the copper wire where the iron touches the joint. I hold the wire steady with a clamp, feed a thin strand of solder into the seam, and watch it spread. When the bead cools, I trim the excess with snips and label the bag of parts.

Bolts sit in the bottom of a wooden crate, sorted by length into small plastic trays. I pick out the three-inch ones, hold each against the bracket, and tighten the nut with a socket wrench. The bracket sits flush against the frame, and I move the stool closer to the cabinet.

Paint drips from the brush in a thin line as I draw it across the old window frame. I work from the top corner downward, keeping each stroke in the same direction. The masking tape along the glass has been pressed down with a thumbnail. Two coats will dry overnight on the ledge by the radiator.

Pliers grip the pin of the old door hinge, and I work it out with a steady push. The hinge separates as the pin slides free, and I lay the two leaves on a rag. I count the screw holes on each leaf and write the number on a scrap of card. Spare hinges hang from a nail above the bench.

Clay turns on the wheel in a slow grey circle while I keep my palms against its side. The walls rise by small increments, and I pinch the rim between two fingers. Water runs down the wheel into a plastic tub, and the bowl takes shape at the centre of the table.

Blue thread is pulled through the eye of a steel needle, and the end is knotted twice. I sit under the lamp by the sewing machine and turn the hem of the trousers inside out. Each stitch goes through the fold at the same distance from the edge, and I count them aloud in groups of five.

Folded in my coat pocket, the shopping list has six items written in pencil. I push the cart past the bread aisle, lift a bag of oranges onto the rack, and check the price tag on the milk. The cashier scans each item, and the till prints a long receipt that curls toward the floor.

Past the paint aisle, I pick a small brass key blank from the labelled rack by the door. I hand it to the clerk, who slides it into the machine on the counter and presses a button. The machine grinds for a few seconds, and a grey film settles on the counter.

Parcels sit on the post office scale while the clerk types the tracking code. I hand over my ID card, sign the form on the glass counter, and take the yellow receipt. The stamps are the square kind with a picture of a lighthouse, and I peel one from the sheet.

Plastic-wrapped shirts hang in rows along the dry cleaner's back wall, each with a paper tag. I give the attendant my ticket, and she checks the number against the list before reaching up for the coat. I count the buttons while she folds it into a paper sleeve, and she clips the receipt to the hanger.

Stacked crates of apples line the front of the market stall, and the brass scale sits on a folding table. I pick six apples, place them in a paper bag, and set the bag on the scale. The stallholder reads the weight aloud and punches the total into a calculator with a large red button.

Coupons fill the front pocket of my wallet, each one dated in small print. At the self-checkout I scan the cereal, and the screen asks me to place the item in the bagging area. I press the green button and lift the receipt from the slot.

Lifting the blue jacket onto the returns counter, I pull the paper tag free and check the price. The clerk scans the barcode, prints a slip, and slides the refund amount under the glass. I fold the slip twice, put it in my wallet, and walk out through the automatic doors.

Shirts are folded in thirds and laid flat in the open suitcase on the bed. I add two pairs of socks in the corner, tuck the charger into the side pocket, and zip the lining closed. The passport and boarding pass go into the front sleeve of my bag.

Grey plastic trays move along the rubber belt at the airport security checkpoint. I place my belt, the coins, and my jacket in a tray and walk through the frame with my arms at my sides. A uniformed officer points to the bin where my laptop goes.

Departures on the platform screen list the next train in small green letters. I check the platform number against my ticket, step back from the yellow edge, and stand by the doors until they open. Inside the carriage I find a seat near the luggage rack and stow my bag above my head.

Marble floors in the hotel lobby reflect the light from a row of brass lamps. At the front desk I give my name, sign the registration card, and receive a plastic key with the room number printed on the sleeve. The lift doors close, and the numbers above the panel count upward one floor at a time.

Spread across the passenger seat, a paper map has its corners weighted with a coffee cup and a guidebook. I trace the route with my finger, read the street names aloud, and mark the turn on the page with a pencil. The road sign ahead shows two kilometres to the next junction.

Sunlight falls through the cabin window of the ferry and lies in a stripe across the bench. I sit in the corner, fasten the zip of my bag, and check the ticket stub in my jacket pocket. The engine vibrates through the deck, and a gull lands on the railing outside the glass.

Rental car paperwork covers the front seat, and the odometer reads 412 kilometres. I adjust the mirrors, fasten the belt, and set the sat nav to the address on the booking slip. The map voice speaks in a flat tone, and the screen shows the route in blue.

Raising the piano lid, I clip the sheet music to the stand and set the metronome to sixty beats per minute. I play the first four bars with my right hand, stop, and write the fingering numbers above each note in pencil. The metronome ticks steadily on the lid, and the keys click under my fingers.

Wet paper takes the blue wash in even layers across the top half of the sheet. I tilt the board so the excess runs toward the bottom edge and collects in a small bead. A square of dry cloth touches the corner, drawing up the extra water. I leave the sheet flat on the table to dry, and it stays there overnight.

Sketchbook open on my knees, I draw the outline of the harbour crane with a 2B pencil. The lines are light at first, and I darken the base where the pier meets the water. Gulls circle above the masts, and the wind lifts the corner of the page, so I hold it down with my thumb.

Six strings on the guitar are tuned one at a time against a small electronic tuner. I pluck each string, watch the needle drift, and turn the peg until it sits in the centre of the dial. The case lies open on the floor with its lid propped against the wall.

Ten of us stand in two rows on the rehearsal stage, sheet music held at chest height. The conductor raises one hand, we inhale together, and the first chord fills the empty hall. I tick the rests in my score and count silently under my breath.

Knitting needles click as the grey yarn slides from the ball through my fingers. I work the second row of the scarf, slipping one stitch and knitting the next, and count the loops on the needle. The pattern sheet is pinned under a jar of buttons on the arm of the chair.

Opening the folder, I find the scanned forms and drag them into a new directory. The file names are numbered in order, and I rename the first three by hand. A progress bar fills across the bottom of the window in thin blue steps.

Above the desk, the router's green lights blink in a steady pattern. The label on its side lists the network name in capitals. I unplug the power cable, count to ten, and plug it back in. Then I watch the modem restart and the status light turn solid.

Keys on the keyboard are worn pale at the centre, where my fingers have rested for years. I type the address into the form, check each letter against the envelope, and press tab to move to the next field. The cursor blinks in the box, and a small grey icon shows the page is saving.

Face down on the kitchen counter, the phone buzzes once against the wood. I turn it over, read the notification, and tap the message open with my thumb. The text lists three dates, and I copy each one into the calendar app.

Software updates download in the background while the laptop sits open on the desk. I click the install prompt, watch the progress circle until it finishes, and close the lid when the restart dialog appears. The screen dims to black, and a small white logo appears in the middle.

An email arrives with a PDF attached and a subject line in plain capitals. I download the file, open it in the viewer, and scroll to the second page where the table begins. I forward a copy to my colleague, add one line of text above the signature, and send it.
